[F5 F6 F8] [SURGE-2 SURGE-3 FARE-0]

[F12 F1 F2 F5 F14] [TH-1 TH-3 SURGE-2]

The overcharge is not explained by any route deviation: the actual distance of 4.0 km equals the optimal 4.0 km (+0.0 km), so no part of the $2.56 is a route-deviation item and the whole difference is attributable to the surge change (F1, F3, F8).

The driver's post-trip statement that he 'doesn't set the price' and drove the app's route (F13) does not answer the notice duty: the only notice in the record is the system surge log at 18:29:30 (F9), and the chat itself contains nothing about the price change (F10, F11, F12).

actions.detail: $2.56 back to the rider's original payment method

what_would_change: Had the rider been notified in-app before pickup with the new multiplier, the revised fare and a free-cancel option, SURGE-2 would leave the higher fare in place.

claims.assertion: The fare was mis-set: the app quoted $15.63 at 1.2× when the rider booked (F6), but the trip was metered at 1.5×, producing a $18.19 charge, i.e. $2.56 above the quote (F7, F8).

The required in-app notice of the higher multiplier was given only at 18:29:30, after the trip had already started at 18:27:00, so it came after the multiplier had taken effect and after the point of pickup (F9, F2).

Even taken at face value the notice does not satisfy SURGE-1 as it omits the item 'new multiplier statement + revised fare + free cancellation' check only in part: it states the 1.5× multiplier and a cancellation option, but the 'option to cancel without penalty' is only stated for a rider already in the car, so the notice requirement is not met at the required time (F9).

The multiplier rose from 1.2× to 1.5× without valid notice, so the whole surge differential is refundable: the trip was billed $18.19 against a $15.63 quote, a differential of $2.56, and the surge component (1.5 − 1.2) × $11.29 = $3.39 exceeds the $2.56 actually charged over the quote, so $2.56 is the refundable amount (F8, F5, F6).

The overcharge is not explained by any route deviation: the actual distance of 4.0 km equals the optimal 4.0 km (+0.0 km), so no part of the $2.56 is a route-deviation item and the whole difference is attributable to the surge change (F1, F3, F8).

The driver's post-trip statement that he 'doesn't set the price' and drove the app's route (F13) does not answer the notice duty: the only notice in the record is the system surge log at 18:29:30 (F9), and the chat itself contains nothing about the price change (F10, F11, F12).

The amount in dispute is small and fully documented — a complete timestamped chat record (F12), complete GPS distance and duration (F1, F2) and a full fare breakdown (F5) — so the case is decidable at system level without the raised 95% threshold: the rider's single fraud flag (flagged_for_repeated_fare_disputes) is history only and cannot decide this case (F14), while the charged amount is under $10 of excess and the surge log is unambiguous.

weaknesses: The in-app notice does state the new 1.5× multiplier and a free-cancellation option (F9); the only defect is timing (18:29:30, after the 18:27:00 start). The driver will argue the rider was told shortly after pickup and stayed in the car, so nothing was hidden.
The rider's own message at 18:23 (F10) and the driver's at 18:24 (F11) show no rider objection to the fare at any point during or after the ride, which the driver may read as acquiescence.

The rider carries a fraud flag for repeated fare disputes (F14), which raises the confidence threshold to 95% under TH-3 and may be used to attack credibility even though the current record is complete and consistent.

The notice text quotes a revised estimate of $19.22 while the final charge was $18.19 (F5, F9); the driver may say the rider was therefore told of, and charged less than, the notified figure, which weakens the 'prejudice' framing of the $2.56 claim.

claims.assertion: The trip is not a route-deviation case: the GPS record shows the actual distance (4.0 km) equalling the optimal route (4.0 km), a deviation of +0.0 km, so no excess distance fare arises under RD-1/RD-2 and the disputed $2.56 is entirely a surge-multiplier difference.

The booking was quoted at 1.2× ($15.63) but the surge multiplier in effect at trip start was 1.5×, and the whole $2.56 overcharge the rider claims is the surge differential, so SURGE-2/SURGE-3 is the only clause that can move money here.

The in-app notice was sent to the rider at 18:29:30, which is after the trip started at 18:27:00, so on the face of the surge log the notice condition in SURGE-1 is not met; the driver does not dispute the timing and accepts that the rider's point on timing is the record.

The notice text itself states all three SURGE-1 items — the new multiplier (“Fares are 1.5× higher right now”), the revised estimated fare (“Your new estimated fare is $19.22”) and free cancellation (“You can cancel for free”) — so if the timing defect is treated as cured or the rider is found to have ridden on, nothing in the wording of the notice is missing.

The driver is not the price-setter: the fare components (base $3.90, distance $5.61, time $1.78, platform $1.25) were computed by the app and the driver's statement that he drove the route the app showed is corroborated by GPS showing zero deviation and a trip 2.4 min faster than estimated.

On any SURGE-2 outcome the maximum differential is capped at the amount the fare exceeds the quote, $2.56 (the arithmetic surge differential of $3.39 being capped), so no refund beyond $2.56 is payable and the ticket amount is the ceiling.

The rider carries a fraud flag (flagged_for_repeated_fare_disputes), which under TH-3 raises the confidence threshold to 95% for any ruling against the driver; the driver's own record (4.7 years, 1253 trips in 90 d, 1 upheld dispute, no route violations) supports upholding the charge rather than penalising him.

There is no rider message in the chat record about price, no acceptance of the higher multiplier and no complaint during the trip — the only messages are the pickup logistics at 18:23–18:24 — so the rider rode to Junction 8 without objecting to the notified 1.5× fare.

No safety issue is disclosed anywhere in the complaint, chat or driver statement; there is no allegation of dangerous driving, harassment or threat, so the case should stay on the fare track and not be diverted under SAFE-1.

weaknesses: The surge log is decisive against my client on timing: F9 records notification at 18:29:30 while the trip started at 18:27:00 (and a trip of only 6.8 min per F2), so RD-5's system detail that notice after the deviation/trip began does not count means SURGE-1 is likely read as not met and SURGE-2 forces a refund of the differential.

F8 states the surge differential as $3.39 while the fare exceeds the quote by only $2.56, and the rider claims exactly $2.56; the rider will argue the cap works in his favour and that he should at minimum recover the full $2.56, leaving my client defending only the label, not the amount.

My client has one upheld dispute in the last 90 days (F15), which the rider can use to suggest a pattern even though F15 shows route: 0 and no-show: 0 and is only relevant to RD-6, not to a surge case.

F7 shows the booking fee of $1.25 was not surged, so my client cannot argue the whole $2.56 was a non-surge component; almost the entire difference is attributable to the multiplier change, which is exactly the SURGE-2 refund trigger.

points.response: Conceded: the GPS record shows 4.0 km actual against 4.0 km optimal (F1, F3), so there is no excess-distance component and the whole $2.56 arises under SURGE-1/SURGE-2, not RD-2.
Accepted as far as it goes: the money clause is SURGE-2/SURGE-3 (F6, F7, F8), and that is exactly the clause my brief relies on — the driver's concession fixes the applicable rule, not the outcome.

This is the driver's own concession of the decisive point: notice at 18:29:30 against a 18:27:00 start (F9, F2) is notice after the multiplier took effect, and SURGE-2 gives a full refund of the differential when the rider is not notified.

The three items can be quoted from the text of F9 without curing the defect: SURGE-1 requires notice 'before or at pickup', and notice timed after the trip started (18:29:30 vs 18:27:00, F9, F2) leaves the condition not met however complete the wording is.

The driver's non-setting of the price is irrelevant to the notice duty: the record shows the only notice is the system log at 18:29:30 (F9) and the chat contains nothing about the fare change (F10, F11, F12), so F13 does not discharge SURGE-1.
The rider agrees the ceiling is $2.56: F8 caps the surge figure (1.5 − 1.2) × $11.29 = $3.39 at the $2.56 by which $18.19 exceeds the $15.63 quote, and the rider asks for that capped amount only.

The fraud flag only raises the threshold to 95% (TH-3); it cannot decide the case, and the record here is complete — timestamped chat (F12), full GPS (F1, F2) and a full fare breakdown (F5) — which is what TH-3's completeness factor measures; the driver's profile (F15) is likewise not a defence to a SURGE-1 notice failure.

Silence in the chat does not convert late notice into notice: the rider's own messages were pickup logistics before the trip (F10, F11) and the only price message on the record is the 18:29:30 system notice after the start (F9, F12), so no in-app acceptance of 1.5× exists.
Agreed — nothing in the complaint, chat or driver statement (F10–F13) raises dangerous driving, harassment or a threat, so SAFE-1 does not apply and the case stays a fare dispute.

Conceded as to the arithmetic and the label: the quote was $15.63 at 1.2× (F6) and the trip metered at 1.5× for $18.19, i.e. $2.56 over the quote (F7, F8) — but the rider's own clause choice, SURGE-3, limits any refund to that surge differential and nothing in the fare breakdown (F5) is a driver-set item.

Conceded: F9 records the notice at 18:29:30 against a 18:27:00 start with a 6.8-minute trip (F2), so on the record the notice came after the trip began and the driver cannot show timely notice under RD-5's own system detail.

Void as to content: the quoted notice states the new multiplier, the revised fare AND free cancellation (F9), and RD-5's bar for a notice's wording is that “a brief reason is enough” — the defect here is timing, not the three items, so this leg of C3 misreads the text.

Agreed on quantum and cap: the arithmetic differential of $3.39 is capped at the $2.56 the fare exceeds the quote (F8), and the driver asks for that same $2.56 so the parties are not apart on amount — only on fault, which SURGE-2 places on the notice, not on the driving.

Accepted, and it defeats any deviation reading against my client: F1/F3 show +0.0 km against the optimal route, so RD-1/RD-2 can add nothing to the $2.56 and no driver violation may be recorded on this trip.

So far as it goes: F13 is a post-trip statement and cannot cure notice, but the rider's point about the app's notice does not touch the driver's separate duty under RD-5, and the chat record (F10–F12) shows the driver did communicate with the rider throughout and that the rider raised no fare objection at any time.

Disputed: TH-3 raises the threshold to 95% because the rider carries a fraud flag for repeated fare disputes (F14), and the rider cannot both carry that flag and ask the court to ignore it; the driver's 4.7-year record with 1253 trips and one non-route dispute (F15) supports the charge standing apart from the notice defect.

Kept, but only as a fact the driver does not contest: F9 fixes the notice at 18:29:30, and no order of the evidence makes a notice sent two and a half minutes into a 6.8-minute trip (F2) a notice given before or at pickup.
Withdrawn as a finding: the flag under TH-3 only raises the threshold for a ruling against the flagged rider — it decides nothing, and the driver asks for the outcome on the record (F1, F5–F9) alone.

notices.text: We reviewed your fare dispute and you're getting $2.56 back. Your ride was quoted at a lower surge rate, but the trip was metered at a higher one. The higher rate started before you were told about it in the app — the notice came after your trip had already begun — so the difference is on us. Your route itself was fine. We'll return $2.56 to the card or account you originally paid with; you don't need to do anything. No action is being taken on your account.

We reviewed the fare dispute on this trip and no violation is being recorded against you. Two things decided it: your route matched the best available route with no extra distance, and the fare difference came from a surge rate change the rider wasn't told about before pickup. That part isn't something you control, so the $2.56 difference is being refunded to the rider's original payment method. Nothing comes out of your earnings for this, and your account is not being flagged.
